In the four years since COVID-19 forced schools to close, education in the United States has faced many problems, including learning loss, lower registration, and student behavior issues. However, perhaps the most [[1]] and long-lasting problem has been the large rise in student absenteeism, which has continued even after schools reopened.
Across the country, about 26 percent of public school students were marked as habitually absent last school year, compared to 15 percent before the pandemic. This is based on the latest data from the American Enterprise Institute. Habitual absence is [[2]] defined as missing 10 percent or more of the school year — about 18 days — for any reason. This increase in absenteeism has [[3]] in schools of all sizes and in all kinds of communities. In richer districts, the number of students regularly missing school has almost [[4]], going from 10 percent before the pandemic to 19 percent in the 2022－2023 school year, according to an analysis by The New York Times. In poorer communities, where absenteeism was already high, the problem has become worse. Around 32 percent of students in the poorest districts missed school regularly in 2022－2023, compared to 19 percent before the pandemic.
The above-mentioned [[5]] show that something important has changed in how American children and families see school, and this change may last for a long time. What used to be a daily routine — waking up, catching the bus, and going to class — is now much less [[6]]. “Our relationship with school became optional,” said Katie Rosanbalm, a psychologist and research professor at Duke University’s Center for Child and Family Policy. The habit of daily school [[7]] and the trust many families had in the school system were broken when schools closed in spring 2020. Even after reopening, things didn’t return to normal. Schools required students to quarantine, offered online learning, and therefore had [[8]] and flexible rules for presence and grading.
Today, student absenteeism is one of the main problems slowing down the country’s [[9]] from pandemic learning loss, according to education experts. Students cannot learn effectively if they are not in school. Also, when many students are missing, it can [[10]] affect the achievements of those who do come to class. This is because teachers have to slow down and adjust lessons to help everyone keep up.
